thread.title: Goldman Signals Blankfein Successor; FAANG Stocks Keep Rising -- ICYMI

author: thestreet.com
title: Goldman Signals Blankfein Successor; FAANG Stocks Keep Rising -- ICYMI
text:
U.S. equities were mixed on Monday, March 12, as the Nasdaq rose 0.36% to a new record, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.62% and S&P 500 fell 0.13%.
Traders received further clarity as to who will lead Goldman Sachs Group Inc. ( GS ) when current Chief Executive Lloyd Blankfein decides to leave. At a February meeting, the board of director picked co-president David Solomon to succeed Blankfein, TheStreet's Bradley Keoun reported, citing a source familiar with the matter. Solomon was chosen over fellow co-president Harvey Schwartz.
We also learned that media personality Larry Kudlow could replace former Gary Cohn as director of the White House's National Economic Council, TheStreet founder Jim Cramer reported on CNBC. Kudlow, who helped craft economic policy during the Reagan administration, has not been formally offered the job but is a leading candidate. Cramer stressed one point about Kudlow in a piece for TheStreet's sister publication Real Money: Larry Kudlow "will do what's right for the most Americans possible."
As Trump works to sort out who will be in charge of the National Economic Council, countries are negotiating to be exempt from U.S. tariffs. Even though the tariffs are causing concerns about a global trade war, the FAANG stocks are all rising this year. Experts say the FAANG companies, which include Facebook Inc. ( FB ) and Amazon.com Inc. ( AMZN ) , are moving higher thanks to their ubiquitous presence in the everyday lives of consumer and relative insulation from global trade concerns, TheStreet's Francesca Fontana reports.
Speaking of FAANG stocks, Apple Inc.'s ( AAPL ) head of service business Eddy Cue suggested that the tech giant won't buy Netflix Inc. ( NFLX ) or Disney ( DIS ) .
And Broadcom Ltd.'s ( AVGO ) pursuit of Qualcomm Inc. ( QCOM ) moved forward as Broadcom works to speed up its plan to be redomiciled in the U.S. by April 3 . But David Marcus takes an in-depth look at how Qualcomm's Cfius gambit could backfire.

Photo of the day: The continuing need for infrastructure improvements
In New York City, one of the most severe winter storms intensified to become the Blizzard of 1888 and crippled the city's infrastructure, leaving rail and road transport unusable for days. In this photo, crews are working to remove snow in Times Square. Even though 130 years have passed since the Blizzard of 1888, winter storms still cause travel delays and can shut down major airports, train stations and roadways. While President Donald Trump campaigned on fixing America's infrastructure, legislation has been slow to progress. But the U.S. still needs new infrastructure, even beyond airports and bridges.
